"haw," itwêwak ôki nôtokêwak, "misawâc namôya ta-kî-nipahikonaw." "kiyâm kêyâpic pêyakwâw pimâcihâtân," itwêwak. ||| “Now,” said those old women, “in any case she will not be able to kill us. Let us revive him once more,” they said.
tâpwê mîna sâsay osîhtâwak ôma mâna ita kâ-pimâcihâcik. ||| Accordingly, again they built that in which they always revived him.
âsay mîna kîkisêpâ ê-nitawâpamât, ê-pimâtisiyit ôhi nâpêsisa awa oskinîkiskwêw, kakwê-nipahêw. ||| When the young woman went to see them in the morning, and the boy was alive, she tried to kill him.
mwêhci ê-wî-nipahât, "awa niwî-nipahik, piyêsiwitik!" âsay mîna itwêw awa nâpêsis. ||| Just as she was about to slay him, “This one means to kill me, O Thunderers!” the boy said again.
tâpwê mistahi pêhtâkosiwak piyêsiwak. ||| Truly with great noise the Thunderers were heard.
"hâw," ômisi itik; "nitawâc ôtê ispimihk kita-isi-kîwêhtahitân," itwêw awa piyêsiw; "âsay nikîsi-ohpikihâw kâ-kî-kîwêhtahak kitihkwatim." "ôma kâ-isinâkosiyân, êkosi wîsta isinâkosiw," itik ôhi piyêsiwa. ||| “Now then,” they said to him; “I shall needs take you home with me aloft,” said the one Thunderer; “I have already brought to maturity your nephew whom I took. Even as I look, so looks he too,” the Thunderer said to him.
tâpwê sipwêhtahik; ati-wêpinik piyêsiwacistwanihk. ||| So he took him away from there; he dropped him into a Thunderer's-nest.
êkwa êkota tahtwâw ê-kî-nêwo-tipiskâyik, êkospîhk êsa ôhi kîs-ôhpikiw ê-piyêsiwit. ||| And there, when four nights had passed, by that time he had grown to maturity as a Thunderer.
kayâs ayîsiyiniwak ômisi kî-pakitinikôwisiwak: kahkiyaw kêkway kî-kitimâkêyimikwak, tahto kêkway kâ-wâpahtamihk, mîna êkâ kâ-wâpahtamoht. ||| Of old men were placed here on earth by the Powers in this wise: they were pitied and befriended by every kind of thing, by as many things as are seen, and by the things that are invisible.
kahkiyaw kêkway kî-pawâtamok. ||| They dreamt of every kind of thing.
ahpô wâkayôsa kî-kiskinôhamâkwak kêkway. ||| Even the bears taught them things.
awêkâ ohci kayâs ayîsiyiniwak kâ-ôh-kî-manitôwicik. ||| That is why the old-time people had manitou power.
êkwa nika-âtayôhkân. ||| Now I shall tell a sacred story.
kîtahtawê yâhki pêyak nâpêw pêyakoyiwa otawâsimisa, êkwa mistahi êsa ê-kitimâkêyimât, mîna ê-miyo-pamihât. ||| Once upon a time, long ago, a certain man had one child, and it seems that he dearly loved him and took care of him.
êkwa kîtahtawê, wayawîtimihk owîkimâkana ê-atoskêyit, kîtahtawê kâ-wanihâcik otawâsimisiwâwa. ||| Then at one time, as his wife was working out of doors, suddenly they lost their child.
namôya kî-kiskêyihtamwak tânisi isi ê-isi-wanihâcik. ||| They could not make out how they had lost track of him.
êkwa êsa mistahi pakwâtamwak, êkwani ê-wanihâcik ôhi otawâsimisiwâwa. ||| They were greatly distressed at having lost their child.
nâpêsisa êsa êwako ani nistam êsa otawâsimisihtâwâw, êwakoni piko. ||| The little boy had been their first child, and the only one.
nama kiskêyihtamok tânisi ê-isi-wanihâcik. ||| They did not know how they had lost him.
êkwa piko itê âta ê-kakwêcihkêmocik, êkwa piyisk pônêyimêwak. ||| Having made inquiry everywhere, at last they gave up.
êkwa awa awâsis nika-âcimâw, tânisi ê-kî-isi-pimâtisit. ||| Now I shall tell of the child, how he managed to stay alive.
êkota êtokê takohtêw; wâkayôs êkwa anihi awâsisa êsa kî-kimotiw. ||| He came to some place or other; it appears that a bear had stolen the child.
êkwa piyisk papâ-wîcêwêw, niyîpiniyiki. ||| Soon he went about with the bear in summer-time.
êkwa kîtahtawê itwêw awa nâpêw: "ahpô êtokê nikosis pimâtisiw!" itwêw mâna. ||| Then at one time that man said, “Perhaps after all my son is alive!” he would always say.
pawâtam âskaw mâna ê-wâpamât okosisa. ||| Every now and then he would dream that he saw his son.
kîtahtawê pêponiyiki mâna kanawêyimik ôhi wâkayôsa. ||| Then in winter-time the bear would take care of the child.
êkosi tahto piko itê ayîsiyiniwak kâ-mawimoscikêyit, âsay kiskêyihtam awa wâkayôs. ||| As often as anywhere men performed their worship, at once the bear knew it.
ahpô kâ-oyaskinahtâkot kiskêyihtam. ||| He knew even when a pipe was filled for him.
ômisi êsa mâna itêw ôhi awâsisa: "nôsisê, âsay mîna ninatomikawin," itwêw êsa. ||| This was what he must have said always to the child: “Grandchild, again I am being invited,” he must have said.
tâpwê êkota kî-ohci-pimâtisiw ana awâsis. ||| So in this way the child stayed alive.
piyisk tâpiskôc ayîsiyiniwa kî-itêyimêw êsa wâkayôsa, ê-owîcêwâkanit. ||| In time he looked upon the bear, his companion, as a human person.
êkosi piyisk mihcêt askiy ê-ohpikihikot, êkwa kêkâc ê-nâpêwit, ômisi itik wâkayôsa: "êkwa kêkâc kikîs-ôhpikin." "wîpac êkwa kita-wayawîn," itik êsa; "kôhtâwiy, anohc kâ-wî-nîpihk, kêkâc mêstihkasoci kôna, êkospî nika-nipahik," itik êsa; "êkota sêmâk wayawîhkan." "'kiya êcika ôma, nôhtâ!' itâhkan, mayaw wâpamaci;" "'nôhtâ, nêwo-tipiskâw namôya ayîsiyiniw nika-wâpamik, iskwêwak têpiyâhk.'" "'kiyawâw mîna namôya ka-wâpaminâwâw.'" "'kîspin wâpamitwâwi iskwêwak, êkosi nika-kotâwaskamikîn.'" "'kakwê-tôta,' kika-itâw kôhtâwiy, wâpamaci," êkosi itwêw awa wâkayôs. ||| Then finally, when the latter had brought him up through many years and he was near to manhood, the bear said to him, “Now you have almost grown up. Soon now you will go outside,” he must have told him; “Your father, this coming spring, when the last of the snow is about to melt away, then your father will kill me,” he must have told him; “then at once do you go outside. ‘And so it is you, my father!’ do you then say to him, as soon as you see him; ‘My father, for four nights let people not see me, women at least. You and my mother, too, I shall not see. If women see me, I shall sink into the earth. Try to do this,’ you will say to your father when you see him” spoke that bear.
"wâpahki ka-takohtêw kôhtâwiy," itwêw êsa awa wâkayôs; "mâka niwî-nipahik," itêw êsa ôhi; "sêmâk takohtêci, kî-nipahici, wayawîhkan," itwêw êsa. ||| “Tomorrow your father will come,” the bear must have said; “But he will kill me,” he must have told the lad; “As soon as he arrives and has killed me, then do you go outside,” he must have said.
tâpwê wiya kisêyiniw awa ê-pê-mâcît, miskawêw wâkayôsa, ita ê-apiyit. ||| Then truly, theold man, for his part, as he came that way on the hunt, found the bear where it was staying.
"tâpwê nimiskawâw wâkayôs," itwêw êsa. ||| “Truly, I have found a bear,” he must have said.
êkwa tâpwê nitawi-nipahêw. ||| Accordingly, he went to kill it.
êkotê mistikwa otinêw, ê-isi-sikwatakahikêt. ||| There he took a long stick and prodded the hole that was in the ground.
tâpwê pê-wayawiyiwa ôhi wâkayôsa. ||| Truly, the bear came forth.
êkwa êkosi isi nipahêw. ||| Then, accordingly, he killed it.
mayaw ôhi wâkayôsa ê-nipahimiht, awa oskinîkiw wayawî-kwâskohtiw. ||| As soon as the bear had been killed, the youth leaped from the hole.
"êwako êcika awa nôhtâwiy!" itwêw êsa. ||| “And so this is my father!” he must have cried.
êkwa, "tânêhki, oskinîkiw, kâ-ôh-isiyan?" ||| Then, “What do you mean, youth?”
"niya ôma, nôhtâ!" itwêw êsa; "wâkayôs ê-kî-kimotamâsk, kâ-oh-kî-wanihiyan," itwêw êsa awa oskinîkiw. ||| “It is I, father!” he must have said; “Because the bear stole me from you, is why you lost me,” the youth must have said.
êkosi ê-itwêt, awa kisêyiniw, "âyimâc niwâpamâw nikosis!" itwêw êsa. ||| When he said this, then the old man must have said, “At last I see my son!”
"nôhtâ, ôma piko kita-isi-nayômiyan," itwêw êsa awa oskinîkiw. ||| “Father, there is only this, that you must carry me on your back,” said the youth. So the old man took his son on his back and carried him.
"êkwa êkotê nêwâw piko kika-âh-âywêpin," itêw êsa ôhtâwiya awa oskinîkiw. ||| “And until we get there, only four times are you to stop and rest,” said the youth to his father.
tâpwê awa kisêyiniw nêyawiskosoci ayiwêpiw ê-nayôhcikêt. ||| So whenever the old man wearied under his burden, he rested, with his load on his back.
mitoni mistahi kosikwatiyiwa, pâskac êsa ostikwânihk ê-tahkopisot, iyikohk ê-miywêyihtahk okosisa ê-wâpamât. ||| The latter was very heavy, the more so, as the old man had tied the strap round his head, so glad was he to see his son.
ohpimê wâhyaw mânokêw êsa. ||| Then far off to one side he set up a tipi.
"nêwo-tipiskâw namôya nika-wâpamikwak ayîsiyiniwak," itwêw êsa. ||| “For four nights people are not to see me,” he said.
tâpwê kisêyiniw osk-âya papâ-nitâhtâmôw apahkwâson mîna apasoya nêwo. ||| So the old man went about borrowing unused tent-covering and four unused tent poles.
êkwa êsa oskinîkiwa otinêw, êkâ cêskwa iskwêwa ê-âpacihâyit; ayisk êsa kayâs kî-kanâtisiw ayîsiyiniw, nayêstaw kanâci-askîhk ê-kî-ayât. mâmaskâc êkwa kanawêyimêw ohpimê okosisa awa kisêyiniw; nêwo-tipiskâw ayisk itik kita-ka-kanawêyimât. ||| [no translation] [no translation] In a way to cause wonder then the old man guarded his son, away from the camp; for he had told him to guard him for four nights.
mwêhci nisto-tipiskâw ê-kanawêyimât, ê-nipât, kayâhtê, "nôhtâ, êkosi êcika ana êkâ wîhkâc kê-wâpamiyan!" itwêw awa oskinîkiw. ||| When he had guarded him for exactly three days and nights, as he slept, suddenly, “Father, and so you are never more to see me!” called the youth.
âsay apisîs piko kî-sâkiskwêw, askîhk ê-kotâwaskamikît. ||| Already his head was but a short way above the earth, into which he was sinking.
êkosi êsa mîna kîhtwâm, "êkosi êsa ani namôya wîhkâc kita-âpisisin ayîsiyiniw!" itwêw êsa awa oskinîkiw; "itâmaskamik kita-nahinâw ayîsiyiniw, ispîhk ohpikihitoci!" itwêw, iskwêyâc ê-pîkiskwêt awa oskinîkiw. ||| Then once more, “And so then, it appears that never again shall a mortal man come back to life!” said that youth; “Under the ground man shall be laid away, as the generations go on!” said the youth, speaking for the last time.
mâka wiya awa iskwêw namôya êsa ohci wâpamêw okosisa, êkosi ê-isi-nipiyit. ||| But as for the woman, she never again saw her son, who in this wise now had died.
êwako pêyak âtayôhkêwin. ||| That is one sacred story.
kîtahtawê ê-mihcêticik ayîsiyiniwak, pêyak okimâw otawâsimisa nisto, nâpêwak. ||| Once upon a time, in a place where there were many people, a certain chief had three children, sons.
nîso ayâwêwak iskwêwa. ||| Two of them had wives.
osîmimâw awa oskinîkiw miyosiw. ||| As for the youngest son, this youth was handsome.
êkosi namôya awiya ayâwêw iskwêwa; mâka mistahi kitimâkêyimik kahkiyaw ostêsa, wîtimwa; tâpiskôc awâsis êkosi pamihâw, osâm ê-kitimâkêyimiht, nisto mîkiwâhpa mâ-mêskoc êkota ê-pîhtokêt. ||| He, then, had no wife, but both of his elder brothers, as well as his sisters-in-law loved him very much; he was cared for like an own child, so beloved was he, as he went in turn to the three tipis.
êkosi kîtahtawê,- ostêsimâwa ôhi ostêsa mistahi kitimâkêyimik ôhi wîtimwa,- êkwa mitoni ê-oskinîkit, kîtahtawê ê-pîhtokêt ôhi ostêsa ostêsimâwa wîkiyihk, pôti pêyakwapiw awa iskwêw. ||| Then at one time his eldest brother's wife was especially fond of him when he had become quite a young man, as once he entered his eldest brother's dwelling, there was that woman alone in the tent.
êkosi ê-wî-wayawît, "cêskwa!" itik wîtimwa; "mîciso," itik. ||| “When, accordingly, he made to go out, “Wait!” his sister-in-law said to him; “First eat a bit,” she told him.
ê-kîsi-mîcisot, ê-wî-sîkahokot, pasikôw, ê-wî-wayawît. ||| When he had eaten, she wanted to comb his hair, but he arose to leave the tent.
"kiwî-sîkahotih ôma!" itik wîtimwa. ||| “Oh, but I meant to comb your hair, you know!” his sister-in-law said to him.
"osâm kipêyakwapin," itêw. ||| “No, for you are alone in the tent,” he told her.
êkosi pasikôw awa iskwêw, iskwâhtêmihk ê-nîpawit, ê-kipiskawât wîtimwa. ||| At that the woman rose to her feet and stood in the doorway, blocking the passage for her brother-in-law.
ômisi itêw: "nîtim, kâ-ôh-kitimâkêyimitân, ê-wî-wîhtamâtân, kita-ôh-owîcimosiyan," itêw, "ayiwâkês ka-kitimâkêyimitin," itêw. ||| she said to him, “Brother-in-law, fond as I have been of you from the beginning, what I want to tell you is, [no translation] [no translation] [no translation] [no translation] [no translation]
êkosi wayawîw awa oskinîkiw. ||| With that the young man went out of the tent.
êkosi ômisi itêyihtam awa iskwêw: "mâskôc wîhtamawâci ostêsa, ta-kisiwâsiw niwîkimâkan," itêyihtam; "nicawâc nika-wîhtamawâw niwîkimâkan," itêyihtam; "nicawâc maywês wîhtamawât ostêsa, niya nika-wîhtamawâw," itêyihtam. ||| Then the woman thought, “If, likely enough, he tells his brother about this, my husband will be very angry,” she thought; “I had better tell my husband,” she thought; “Before he tells his brother, I had better tell him myself,” she thought.
ê-pîhtokêyit owîkimâkana, ômisi itêw: "niwîkimâkan, namôya êkosi ê-kî-itêyihtamân, kisîm kâ-ôh-kitimâkêyimak." "anohc ê-pîhtokêt, nikakwêcimik ta-nôcîhkawit," itêw; "mitoni nimâmaskâtên ê-isi-kitosit, kâ-ôh-wîhtamâtân." "êkosi namôya êkwa nika-kî-kitimâkêyimâw kisîm," itêw. ||| When her husband came into the tent, she told him thus: “My husband, it was not in this way that I meant it, when from the first I showed affection to your younger brother. [no translation] she told him, “I was greatly surprised when he spoke in this way to me; that is why I am telling you of it. And so now I shall no longer be able to feel any fondness for your younger brother,” she told him.
sêmâk pakwâtam awa nâpêw. ||| At once that man was distressed.
"namôya êkosi ê-kî-itêyihtamân, 'kakwê-kitimâkêyim nisîm,' kâ-ôh-ititân mâna," itêw. ||| “It was not in this way that I meant it, when I would say to you, ‘Try to be fond of my young brother’,” he told her.
êkosi awa oskinîkiw nêpêwisiw ê-kî-itikot wîtimwa. ||| Now the young man was embarrassed by what his sister-in-law had said to him.
namôya wî-ay-itohtêw. ||| He did not feel like going there any more.
"tâpwê êtokê êkosi ê-itêyihtahk nisîm, êkwa êkâ kâ-pîhtokêt," itêyihtam awa ostêsimâw. ||| It really seems that my young brother did intend something like that, seeing that he does not come to my tent any more,” thought that eldest brother.
mâka kisiwâsiw ôma kâ-itikot owîkimâkana. ||| He was very angry at what his wife had told him.
kîtahtawê wîhkâc ê-itohtêt awa oskinîkiw, ê-wî-pîhtokêt, wâpamik ostêsa. môhkomân otinam, "nika-nipahâw nisîm," ê-itêyihtahk. ||| Then at one time, when the young man, after a long interval, did go there, as he was about to step into the tent, his eldest brother saw him.
ê-pê-pîhtokêyit, ê-wî-tahkamât, asêpayihôw awa oskinîkiw. têpiyâhk apisîs pikwâhok. namôya mitoni pikwâtayêhok. ||| He seized a knife, thinking, “I shall kill my young brother.” As the latter was coming in, and he made to stab him, the young man threw himself back.
êkosi isi wayawiyâmôw awa oskinîkiw, ê-ma-mawimoyit wîtimwa ôhi kâ-misimikot. ||| He managed to run the knife into him a little ways. He stabbed him in the abdomen, not deeply.
kotakak iskwêwak ê-wayawîcik môskîstawêwak ôhi nâpêwa, ê-nawaswâtâyit osîmiyiwa. ||| The youth fled out of the tent; his sister-in-law who had slandered him kept crying out the while.
nawatinâw awa nâpêw, ê-miciminiht. êkosi pôyôw. ||| Other women came out of their tipis and ran at the man who was pursuing his young brother.
ê-pîhtokêt wîkiwâhk, kotakak nâpêwak pîhtokêwak, ê-kitahamâht. ||| So he gave up his intent. He was taken home. When he went into his tipi, other men came in to admonish him.
"tânêhki kâ-ôh-tôtawât osîma, ê-kiskêyimiht ê-kitimâkêyimât?" ||| “Why has he done thus to his younger brother, when he is known to be fond of him?”
âcimôw: "ê-kakwêcimât wîtimwa ê-wî-owîcimosit, êwako ohci kâ-ôh-tôtawak," itêw. ||| He told his story: [no translation] is why I have done this to him,” he told them.
êkosi awa oskinîkiw ôhtâwiya wîkiyihk êkotê pîhtokahâw, ê-nanâtawihiht. ||| Then the young man was brought into his father's dwelling and given medical treatment.
piyisk kinwêsk ayâw, ê-wîsakêyihtahk, ohôsîmimâwa ostêsa ê-pamihikot êkwa wîtimwa. nîso ayâwêyiwa iskwêwa. ||| It turned out that he stayed a long time, suffering pain, and nursed by the younger of his elder brothers, and by his sisters-in-law.
êwakonik mistahi pakwâtamwak ê-tôtâmiht ôhi oskinîkiwa wîtimowâwa, osâm tâpiskôc otawâsimisiwâwa ê-isi-kitimâkêyimâcik ôhi. ||| This brother had two wives. They were very much distressed at what had been done to the youth, their brother-in-law, for they loved him like an own child.
"mâskôc ahpô ta-nipiw," itêyihtâkosiw awa oskinîkiw. ||| “Likely enough he will die,” was the general thought concerning that young man.
ê-âta-nanâtawihiht, piyisk kinwêsk âhkosiw. ||| In spite of the curative treatment give him, for a long time, in the outcome, he was ill.
piyisk kîwêhtahêw awa osîma wîkiwâhk, ê-wî-pamihât, "osâm ê-kwatakihtât nôhtâwiy mîna nikâwiy, ê-pamihâcik nisîma," ê-itêyihtahk; "mâka êkotê wêtinahk nika-pamihânân," ê-itêyihtahk. tâpwê pamihêwak osîma. ||| At last the man took his young brother to his own tent, to nurse him, thinking, “It is too much of a strain for my father and mother to nurse my young brother; over here we can nurse him undisturbed.” Accordingly, they nursed his young brother.
awa kâ-kî-tahkamât osîma nama wîhkâc nitawâpamêw, mîna owîkimâkana. ||| The man who had stabbed his brother never came to see him, nor did his wife.
napâwi kaskêyihtam, ê-nôhtê-wâpamât awa iskwêw kâ-kî-misimât wîtimwa. ||| Now that it was too late, the woman who had slandered her brother-in-law was sorry and wanted to see him.
"nika-itohtân," êtâci owîkimâkana, êkosi ê-pakamahokot, ê-kâhkwêyihtahk awa, kâ-ôh-tôtawât osîma. ||| But whenever she said to her husband, “Let me go there,” he would beat her, for he was jealous, and even for that had done thus to his brother.
piyisk ati-miyw-âyâw awa oskinîkiw. ||| At last the young man was on the way to recovery.
"kêhcinâ miyw-âyâyâni, ahpô nika-nipahik nistês." "miyw-âyâyâni, nika-sipwêhtân." "kiyâm piko itê wî-misi-wanâtisiyâni," itêyihtam awa oskinîkiw, ê-ati-miyw-âyât. ||| “Surely, when I get well, my brother will go even so far as to kill me. If I get well, I shall go away from here. What matter if somewhere or other I go to my destruction?” thought the youth as he got better.
iyikohk êkwa ê-miyw-âyât, mâka namôya wîhkâc nipâyiwa ôho wîtimwa êkwa ostêsa, mâ-mîskoc ê-kanawêyimikot, têpiskâki êkâya ê-nipâyit. ||| But when he became well, those sisters-in-law of his and his brother never slept, but took turns in attending to him and not sleeping of nights.
kîtahtawê ôhi osîmimâwa wîtimwa, ê-wî-wâpaniyik, êkâ ê-na-nipâyit, kiskêyimêw ê-nôhtêhkwasiyit. ||| Once, when the younger of his sisters-in-law was watching, toward dawn, he perceived that she was sleepy.
ômisi itêw: "nîtim!" ||| He said to her, “Sister-in-law!”
"mahti pahkêkinos pêtâ êkwa astis êkwa oskâcihk." ||| “Please give me a small piece of leather and a sinew and an awl.”
"tânisi ê-wî-tôtaman?" itik. ||| “What do you want to do?” she asked him.
"nimaskisin ê-pîkopayik, ê-wî-mîsahamân," itêw. ||| “It is my moccasin which is torn that I want to mend,” he told her.
"pê-kêcikona;" "niya nika-kaskikwâtên." "namôya wîhkâc kika-kaskikwâtison, ahpô ê-miyomahcihoyan;" "wâwîs cî êkwa ka-pamihison, âyimâc ê-pimâtisiyan?" itêw; "misawâc apisîs ôma," itêw. ||| “Take it off and give it to me; let me sew it. You are never to do your own sewing, even when you are well; do you suppose you will be allowed to do your work now that you are barely alive?” she asked him; “In any case, this is a little thing,” she told him.
mâka mistahi nôhtêhkwasiw awa oskinîkiskwêw. ||| But the woman was very sleepy.
piyisk miyêw ôhi kâ-nâh-nitotamâkot wîtimwa. ||| At last she gave her brother-in-law what he asked of her.
êkwa manisam awa oskinîkiw, ê-oyisahk ôma pahkêkinos. ||| Then the young man cut from it, cut the leather to shape.
kâ-wâpamât wîtimwa ê-nipâyit, kahkiyaw êwakoni otinam; opîhtatwâna otinêw. ||| As soon as he saw that his sister-in-law was asleep, he took all of those things; he took his quiver.
êkosi isi ê-wayawît, ê-sipwêhtêt, "kiyâm nânitaw itê nika-misi-wanâtisin." "misawâc tahki nika-pakwâtik nistês," ê-itêyihtahk. ||| Thus he went out of the tent and away, thinking, “I may as well go to my destruction, it matters not where. In any case my brother will always despise me.”
êkosi pikonita itê isi sipwêhtêw. ||| So he set out, with no destination.
iyikohk ê-pêkopayit awa nâpêw, namwâc wâpamêw osîma. ||| When that man woke up, he did not see his young brother.
owîkimâkana koskonêw, "tâniwâ nisîm?" ê-itât. ||| He roused his wives, asking them, “Where is my brother?”
"aspin ôma, 'nika-kaskikwâtên nimaskisina,' ê-itwêt, ê-âta-na-nitotamawak, êkâ ê-wî-miyit, piyisk nimiyâw cita-âpacihtât." "êkosi ê-isi-nahisiniyân, êkosi êtokê ninipân, êkâ kâ-ôh-kiskêyimak ê-wayawît," itêw. ||| “The last I know was that he said he was going to mend his moccasins; and though I kept asking him to give them to me, he would not do it, until at last I gave him the things he wanted to use. Then, when I lay down, I must have fallen asleep and not noticed his going out,” the one told him.
kiskêyihtam ê-sipwêhtêyit awa nâpêw osîma. ||| The man knew that his young brother had gone away.
nitawi-wîhtamawêw ôhtâwiya, ta-nitonâmiht osîma, ê-itêyihtahk, ayisk ôhtâwiya ê-okimâwiyit, ê-tipêyihtamiyit ôtênaw. ||| He went and told his father, that his brother might be looked for, for his father was a chief, and had power over the camp.
êkosi wayawîw awa kisêyiniw, ê-wîhtahk ê-wanihâcik okosisa, ta-mâmawi-nitonâmiht, ê-sîhkihkêmot. ||| So the old man went out of his tent and announced that they had lost his won, and ordered a general search for him.
awa oskinîkiw âsay wâhyaw ayâw. ||| By this time the youth was far off.
ita mistahi ê-sakâyik, êkota sêskisiw. ||| Where there was heavy timber, he went into the woods.
mêkwâ-sakâhk êkota nahapiw. ||| Well into the woods he sat down.
piyisk kawisimôw, "êkâ nika-miskâkawih!" ê-itêyihtahk. ||| At last he lay down, thinking, “May I not be found!”
êkwa ôki ayîsiyiniwak misiwê nitonikêwak. ||| Those people searched everywhere.
kiyikaw sakâhk ê-nitonâht, nama miskawâw. ||| He was sought here and there in the woods, but not found.
iyikohk mistahi ê-tipiskâyik, êkwa sipwêhtêw awa oskinîkiw. ||| When it was entirely dark, the youth set out.
namôya kiskêyihtam tânitê kâ-isi-sipwêhtêt. ||| He did not know in what direction he was going.
iyikohk mîna ê-wî-wâpaniyik, ita ê-pasahcâyik, ê-sakâyik, êkota mîna kawisimôw. ||| When daylight was again near, again he lay down, in a wooded ravine.
sakâhk êkwa ôki mîna nitonikêwak ayîsiyiniwak; mâka âsay wâhyaw ayâw awa oskinîkiw. ||| Now, those people searched also in the woods; but by this time the youth was far away.
nâh-nôhtaw ohci wâyonîwak kâ-nitonawâcik. ||| The searchers all turned back before they had come upon him.
kapê-kîsik nipâw awa oskinîkiw. ||| The young man slept all day.
iyikohk ê-otâkosik, êkoyikohk pêkopayiw. ||| In the evening he awoke.
kîtahtawê kâ-pêhtahk ê-matwê-mâtôwiht. ||| Presently he heard someone weeping.
êkwa ê-wî-kakwê-wâpamât kâ-mâtoyit, kâ-nisitawêyimât ostêsa, êkota ê-ispatinâyik ê-na-nîpawiyit. ||| When he made to see the one who was weeping, he recognized his brother, standing motionless on a hill.
êkosi âhci piko kâsôhtawêw. ||| So he kept hiding from him.
wiya ohci kâ-ôh-mâtoyit, ê-wanihikot. ||| His brother was weeping for him, because he had lost him.
piyisk ê-wî-tipiskâyik, aspin ê-kîwêyit, iyikohk êkây ê-pêhtawât, wîsta êkwa sipwêhtêw, ê-tipiskâyik. ||| At last, as darkness was coming on, his brother departed to go home; when he heard him no more, he, too, set out, in the dark.
êwako mîna kapê-tipisk pimohtêw. ||| All of that night again he walked.
êyikohk ê-wî-wâpaniyik, konita ita kawisimôw, "misawâc wâhyaw nitayân êkwa," ê-itêyihtahk; "misawâc namôya awiyak nika-wâpamik," ê-itêyihtahk. iyikohk ê-pêkopayit, âsay ispi-kîsikâyiw. ||| Toward daybreak, he lay down, wherever he happened to be, thinking, “Now I am surely far off; now surely no one will see me.” When he awoke, it was already bright day.
"kiyâm ê-kîsikâk êkwa nika-pimohtân," itêyihtam. ||| “I may as well walk by daylight now,” he thought.
nama wîhkâc mîcisôw, aspin kâ-sipwêhtêt. ||| He had not eaten from the time he set out.
kapê-kîsik ê-pimohtêt, iyikohk ê-ati-tipiskâyik, mîna konita ita kawisimôw. âsay nôhtêhkatêw. ||| He walked all day, and when darkness was falling, again lay down where he happened to be.
mîna ê-wâpaniyik, âsay mîna sipwêhtêw. ||| By this time he was hungry. The next morning he went on.
namôya mâka kiskêyihtam tânitê ta-itohtêt. ||| He did not know, however, where he was going.
nama wîhkâc kî-papâ-wâpahtam ôma askiy. ||| He had never gone about seeing the world.
êkosi mistahi nôhtêhkatêw. ||| He was very hungry now.
nama wîhkâc ê-tipiskâyik êkwa pimohtêw, piko ê-kîsikâyik. ||| Now he never walked at night, but only in daytime.
piyisk êtokê wâhyaw êkwa ayâw, wiya tahto-kîsikâw ê-pimohtêt. ||| In time he must have gone very far, walking every day, as he did.
kîtahtawê kiskêyihtam ê-yîkicikâwît, êkwa êsa ani mistahi ê-kawâhkatosot. ||| Presently he felt himself growing feeble; indeed, he was almost prostrate with hunger.
nama wîhkâc ayisk mîcisôw, ohcitaw êkâ ê-wî-nipahât kêkway ta-mîcit. ||| For he never ate, purposely refraining from killing anything he might eat.
"yahô, tâpwê miyâmay konita niwî-nipahâhkatoson." "nawac kêkway ta-nipahikoyân, êkosi ta-miywâsin." "mîna êkâ kêkway nipahikoyâni, niya kîkway ahpô nipahtâyâni, mîna kotak kêkway miskamâni ta-kî-âpacihtâyân, nika-kîwân, nânitaw ohtinamân," ê-itêyihtahk; "nicawâc êkwa kêkway wâpahtamâni ta-kî-mîciyân, nika-kakwê-nipahtân," itêyihtam. ||| “Oh, it really looks as if I should simply starve to death. It would be better if some creature should kill me. But if nothing kills me, and if I, by any chance, kill something, and if, besides, I find something that I can use, then I shall go home, if from any place I get something,” he thought; “If I see anything I can eat, I suppose I had better try to kill it,” he thought.
mâka nama kêkway kî-wâpahtam. ||| But he did not see anything.
kîtahtawê êkwa namôya kî-mîhkawikiw, osâm ê-kawâhkatosot, piko mistik ohci ê-saskahohtêt, ê-nêsôwâhkatosot êkwa. ||| Then in time he could no longer walk with any speed, so weak was he from hunger; he hobbled along leaning on a stick, feeble from starvation.
kîtahtawê nîswâw ê-kî-nipât, êkoyikohk kâ-wâpamât pihyêwa, "nika-kakwê-nipahâw, êkwa kê-mîcisoyân," ê-itêyihtahk. tâpwê pimwêw; nipahêw. ||| Presently, after two nights, at last he saw a partridge, and thought, “I shall try to kill it, that I may eat.” So he shot an arrow at it; he killed it.
otinêw êkwa, ê-pa-paskopitât. ||| He took it and plucked off the feathers.
kisiwâk ôta ispatinâyiw; awasitê wâpahtam ê-sakâyik. ||| Near by was a rise in the land; he saw that there was a wood beyond.
"êkota nika-kakwê-kapêsin," itêyihtam, ê-sipwêhtêt. ||| “I shall try to camp there for the night,” he thought and set out.
ê-ati-sâkêwêt, kâ-wâpahtahk mîkiwâhpis ê-cimatêyik. ||| When he got to the top of the hill, he saw a little lodge standing there.
"tâpwê nimiywêyihtên ayîsiyiniwak ta-wâpamakik," itêyihtam. ||| “Truly, I am glad that I shall see some people,” he thought.
namwâc mâ-mitonêyihtam ta-misi-wanâcihikot, "iyâyaw êkwa kê-pimâtisiyân; niwî-nipahâhkatosoh," ê-itêyihtahk. ||| He did not consider that they might destroy him; “Now I am surely destined to live; otherwise I should have died of hunger,” he thought.
ê-takohtêt, nama kêkway wâpahtam wayawîtimihk, kâ-matwê-pîkiskwêwiht, "ta-tawâw, nôsisimis! ||| When he reached the place, he saw nothing outside the lodge, but someone spoke for him to hear, “Come in, grandchild!
pîhtokê!" kâ-matwêhitwêyit nôtokêsiwa. ||| Come right in!” said an old woman, for him to hear.
ê-pîhtokêt, awîna ôhi kî-pêyakoyiwa. ||| When he entered, why, there she was, all alone.
"nôsisimis, nôsisimis," ê-itikot, "mâni ê-âyimaniyik itê kâ-itohtêt!" kâ-itikot; "nêtê ohci-api," itik. ||| “My grandchild, my grandchild,” she said to him; “Heavens, it is a dangerous place whether he is bound!” she told him; “Sit down over there,” she told him.
êkwa miyêw ôhi pihêwa. ||| Then he gave her that partridge.
"nôhkô, awa môwâhkan," itêw. ||| “Grandmother, take this to eat,” he told her. “Truly, my grandchild is giving me a treat!” she said to him; “And so my grandchild has been going hungry! I shall cook something for him,” she said to him.
ê-apisîsisiyit askihkosa kâ-akotâyit, êkwa nîso ê-apisâsiniyiki wiyâsisa ê-pakastawêhamiyit, nîso mîna mînisisa, "ninôhtêhkatâh, apisîs kâ-pakâhtâkohkêt nôhkom!" itêyihtam. ||| After hanging up a tiny little kettle, she put into the water two tiny bits of meat and two little berries; “Here am I, starving, and my grandmother puts so little food in her kettle!” he thought.
êkosi ômisi itik: "nôsisê, âyiman itê kâ-itohtêyan." "namôya wîhkâc pê-kîwêw awiyak, êkotê êtohtêci." "âta mâna nikitahamawâwak oskinîkiwak," itwêyiwa; "nôsisê, nawac ta-kîwêyan, wâpahki." "âyiman ôma itê kâ-itohtêyan," itik. ||| At once she said to him, “Grandchild, it is an evil place to which you are going. Never does anyone return, when people go there. In vain do I always try to dissuade the young men,” she said; “Grandson, you had better go back home in the morning. It is an evil place to which you are going,” she told him.
"yahâ, nôhkô, osâm âsay wâhyaw nitayân." "ahpô ôma konita kê-nipahâhkatosoyân, mâka wiya êkotê takohtêyâni, misi-wanâcihikoyâni kîkwaya, ta-miywâsin." "ispîhci konita ta-nipahâhkatosoyân, namôya nika-kî-kîwân," itêw. ||| “Oh, grandmother, I am too far along by now. As it is, I shall die of hunger, to no purpose; if I reach that place and something or other destroys me, it will be as well. If to no purpose I starve to death on the way, then too I shall not reach home,” he told her.
"hâw, nôsisimis, nêwo-tipiskâw ôta ayâ, mâka ka-kiskinôhamâtân kîkway, tânisi tita-ayîhtiyan," itik. ||| “Very well, my grandchild, stay here four nights, and I shall at any rate teach you something as to the way you shall do,” she told him.

tâpwê yîkicikâwîw ê-mîcisot nôsisim!" itik. ||| Truly my grandson is a poor eater!” she said to him.

kîtahtawê ômisi itik: "nôsisê, kinêstosinâtokê!" "kiyâm pita nipâ," itik. ||| Presently she said to him, “Grandson, you must be tired! You had better sleep now,” she told him.

nikîsi-paminawason," itwêyiwa. ||| I have finished cooking,” she said.
êkosi ê-pê-pakitinamâkot ôhi otaskihkosiyiwa, êkwa ê-mîcisot. ||| Then she brought her tiny kettle and set it before him, and he ate.
piyisk kîspôw, "tâpwê âh-apisîs mîcisôw nôsisimis!" ê-itikot. ||| After a while he had enough, and, “Truly, little at a time does my grandchild eat!” she told him.
"êkoyikohk nôhkô, ê-kîspoyân mâna," itêw. ||| “When I have as much as this, I am always filled,” he told her.
êkosi kapê-kîsik êkota ay-ayâw. ||| Then he stayed there all day, for several days.
wêtâkosiniyiki, kâ-mîcisotwâwi, êkosi ê-nikamohikot, iyikohk êhkêyimikoci, "kawisimo!" ê-itikot. ||| In the evening, when they had eaten, she would teach him songs, and when she thought he had enough of it, she would say to him, “Go to bed!”
ê-kî-nêwo-tipiskâyik, "hâw, êkwa, nôsisê, êkwa ka-sipwêhtêyan," itik. ||| When the fourth night had come, “Now them, my grandson, the time has come for you to go,” she told him. By this time he felt in good health again, when for four nights his grandmother had fed him; he was quite stout by this time; he no longer was feeble from starvation.
ômisi itik ôhkoma: "nôsisê, âta ôma êkosi ê-isi-kiskinôhamawakik oskinîkiwak, mâka namôya nitâpwêhtâkwak, kâ-ôh-mâh-misi-wanâtisicik." "wiyahpitâci, êkoyikohk êkwa, 'nahi, nôsisê!' kika-itik." "êkâya tâpwêhtawâhkan." "'têhtahin!' itâhkan." "kîspin êwako tôtamani, kika-pimâtisin; ka-sâkôcihâw." "nêwo-tipiskâw anima kiyi-ayâyin, êkosi nêwomitanaw misatimwak ta-paskiyawat ana kisêyiniw." "âta ani kêtimâkinawakwâwi oskinîkiwak, êkosi ôma êsi-kiskinôhamawakik, mâka namôya nitâpwêhtâkwak." "misahkamik oskinîkiwak êkâ kâ-ôh-pê-kîwêcik, ê-ati-misi-wanâcihikocik," itik; "mistahi kaskêyihtam kôhtâwiy kikâwiy kistês kîtimwak aniki kâ-kitimâkêyimiskik," itik. ||| His grandmother told him as follows: “My grandson, even though I have taught young men in this same way, they did not follow my instructions, and therefore, went, one after another, to their ruin. If you heed my words, you will fare well; but if he dissuades you to whom you will come, he will destroy you,” she told him; “At any rate, carry this on your person,” she told him, giving him the skin of a beaver-owl; “This thing, my grandson, you will keep for four nights. If he does not destroy you, when you are sleepy, ‘Grandfather, let me lie down a while!’ you will say to him. If he says ‘Yes,’ you will place this thing on your chest. ‘Now then, if my grandfather speaks to you, answer him! I shall sleep. When daylight is near, then wake me!’ you will say to this thing. And this,” she told him, “You will spread under you as you lie,” his grandmother told him, as she gave him her breech-clout; “Only by doing thus will you be able to overcome that old man. And when you are near there, as you go along you will pick up a stick, a stick that is not large. When you have slept twice on the way, you will see water. Not at all will you be able to see where that body of water has its end,” she told him; “And so, after the day is past noon, then you will have come near that lake. It will be level land. You will see a very small rise in the land. To it you will go; there you will seat yourself. When you have seated yourself, there close to the lake you will see a tall man come into view. He will be dressed like a woman. You will not see his feet. When he comes to where you are, ‘Ha, grandson, go back home! The one you have come to fetch you may take home with you,’ he will say to you. At that a handsome white horse will come forth into view. ‘There, this one I give to you. Go home!’ he will say to you. Do you not heed his words. Say this to him: ‘It is not this one I desire,’ you will say to him. Then, ‘Oh, yes, that is true, grandson!’ he will say to you. He will take you back with him to the place from which he came. ‘Go bring the saddle, that you may ride home,’ he will say to you, when you reach his dwelling; ‘Go, grandon, and take it! Go right in! It is a beaded saddle,’ he will tell you. If you take it, persuaded by his speech, that horse will indeed come there. ‘Take him; saddle him’ he will say to you. When you have saddled him, ‘Mount!’ he will tell you; ‘Go home!’ he will tell you. If he persuades you, and you mount, try as you may to depart, that horse will take you off straight to the lake. You will not be able to manage him. In the end he will go under the water. You must wait for a different horse to come up from the water; that one will destroy you,” she told him; “Do not heed his words,” she told him; “Four nights you will stay there. If you heed this which I tell you, you will overcome him, if you stay there four nights. But when you are sitting on that little mound, and he comes walking to where you are, if them you do not heed this which I have told you, he will talk you into acting against your will. ‘Go ahead, walk right in!’ he will tell you. ‘Do you enter first!’ you will say to him. If you persuade him, as he is about to go in, just as he enters the dwelling, with that little stick you will lift up his skirt. You will see his feet. You will see that his feet are like a horse's. ‘Heavens! What do my grandfather's feet look like!’ you will say to him. ‘What do they look like, grandson? Do you mean to say that you see them?’ he will ask you. ‘Yes! Your feet look like horses' hoofs,’ you will answer him. My grandchild, be sure, by all means, to try to see his feet. If you see them, then indeed you will overcome him. But if you do not see them, if you do not do as I now am teaching you, he will overcome you,” she told him; “But if you see his feet, then indeed you will overcome him. Then if you succeed in staying there four nights, then every day he will give you one horse. ‘Go home!’ he will tell you. You will not obey him. It is really only if you defeat him that he will give you those horses. When the fourth night of your stay has passed, ‘Now, grandfather, it is your own horse, the stallion, that I have come to fetch,’ you will say to him. ‘Very well,’ he will answer you. By the door there will be lying an ugly saddle; and the rawhide bridle, strung together of small ends, will be ugly. For these you will ask him. ‘It is those other saddles that are good, and those bridles,’ he will say to you. Do not heed his words. He will defeat you with this one thing, even though you go unharmed through the four nights,” she told him; “If you persuade him this time too, ‘Very well then, grandson; now for my own horse which you have come to fetch!’ he will say to you. Then he will go out of the lodge. He will take that very same ugly saddle and bridle. Then you will follow him. He will stand beside the lake. ‘My horse, come to land!’ he will call. At once the water will rise up high; it will look as if it were boiling. At last a stallion with a bay coat will come out of the water. It will come to the land. It will drag its tail on the ground. And its mane, here, too, will almost reach the ground. When it comes to land, ‘There, grandson, take him!’ he will say to you. Do not obey him. ‘Take him for me!’ you will say to him. When he has taken it, ‘Saddle him for me!’ you will say to him. When he has saddled it, then, ‘Here you are, grandson!’ he will say to you. Do not heed his speech. ‘Put me on his back!’ do you then say to him. If you do this, you will live; you will defeat him. But if you take the horse before he has set you on its back, that horse will destroy you; it will eat you,” she told him; “But if he puts you on its back, then indeed you will come home. Having stayed there four nights, you will win forty horses from that old man. But though again and again I have taken pity on young men and instructed them even in this wise, yet they have not obeyed me. That is why any number of young men have not returned from there, but have been destroyed by him,” she told him; “Very sad is your father, and your mother, and your elder brother, and those your sisters-in-law who are fond of you,” she told him.
êkwa sipwêhtêw êkwa, ê-kî-miyikot ôhi kâ-wî-miyikot. ||| Then he set out, after she had given him the things she wished to give him.

pita nika-wayawîn," itêw omosôma. ||| First let me go outside a moment,” he said to his grandfather.

"hâh, êkosi êwako kâ-wî-kiskêyihtamân, 'tânêhki kâ-ôh-kî-tôtawit?' ê-itêyimitân." "hâw, awa ôta kâ-sakahpisot kîwêhta, ê-miyitân," itêw. ||| “Dear me, no, brother! I know how much you loved me. It is true that when I came and entered your tipi your wife was sitting alone. When I wanted to go out again, ‘First eat,’ she told me. ‘No, you are alone in the tent,’ I said to her. ‘Oh, it does not matter that I am alone, seeing how fond we are of you.’ So I sat down and she gave me food. When I had eaten, and was rising to my feet, ‘First let me comb your hair,’ she said to me. ‘No, you are alone in the tent,’ I said to her. When I tried to go out, she blocked me in the doorway. [no translation] she said to me; ‘If you do as I ask, much as I have loved you, I shall take even better care of you.’ ‘Why, how could I do such a thing? My brother is so good to me,’ I said to her. ‘He does not need to know of it,’ she answered me. Then, when she stepped aside, I came out. I was embarrassed, for I looked upon all my sisters-in-law even as upon my mother, when they were so good to me,” he told him; “It was for this reason that for a long time I did not come into your tent, because she who sits here had put me to shame. Well, this is what I wanted to know, for, ‘Why has he done this to me?’ was my thought concerning you. Now then, take home with you the animal that is tethered here; I give him to you,” he told him.
"hay hay!" itwêw awa ostêsimâw. ||| “Thanks, thanks!” said the elder brother.
"niyâ, kîwêtân!" itêw owîkimâkana. ||| “Come, let us go home!” he said to his wife.
ê-ati-wayawîcik, nêtê ê-takohtêcik wîkiwâhk, ê-kî-sakahpitât awa misatimwa, êkwa itêw owîkimâkana, "sâkêwêtân ôma kâ-ispatinâk," itêw. ||| When they had gone out, as they came to their tent yonder, after tying up the horse, he said to his wife, “Let us go over that hill there.”

"kêkâc kâ-kî-nipahtwâsoyân!" itêw, môhkomân ê-otinahk, ê-ta-tahkamât, ê-nipahât owîkimâkana. ||| When they had sat down there, “And so it appears that you are of a most evil nature! It appears that you were the one who had that desire! Remember, I loved my little brother! And here I came near killing what was dear to me!” he said to her, and taking a knife, stabbed her repeatedly, and killed her.
êkwa awa awa oskinîkiw ôhi wîtimwa, kâ-kî-nitotamawât pahkêkinos oskinîkiskwêwa, êwakoni êkwa miyik ostêsa owîkimâkaniyiwa. ||| Then that youth was given his sister-in-law, the young woman whom he had asked for a piece of leather; his elder brother, her husband, gave her to him.

kêtahtawê êsa wâpos kâh-kimotiw pakânisa. ||| Once upon a time a rabbit used to steal nuts.
êkwa kisiwâhêw ôhi ka-kimotamawât. ||| He angered the people from whom he stole them.
"tânisi kê-tôtawâyahk?" itwêwak. ||| “Shat shall we do to him?” they asked.
"ka-wanihikamawânaw." ||| “Let us set a snare for him.”
êkwa wâpos ê-ispahtât, micimoskiwêw. ||| Then when Rabbit ran there, he got stuck in the gum.
êkwa ôki ayîsiyiniwak, "tânisi kê-tôtawâyahk!" ||| Then those people, “What shall we do with him?”
"mônahipânihk ahpô okâminakasîskâhk ka-pîhciwêpinânaw?" ||| “Shall we throw him into a well or into the brambles?”
"êkwa êsa ka-kakwêcimânaw tânita kâ-isiwêpinâyahk." "tânima kostahki ôta ka-isiwêpinânaw." ||| “Let us ask him where we are to throw him. Whichever he fears, there we shall throw him.”
êkwa nâtêwak wâposwa; êkwa kakwêcimêwak. ||| Then they fetched rabbit and questioned him.
"tânita kê-isiwêpinitâhk, mônahipânihk ahpô okâminakasîskâhk?" ||| “Where shall we throw you, into a well or into the brambles?”

"êkota ka-isiwêpinânaw," itwêwak. ||| “There we shall throw him.” they said.
otihtinêwak wâposwa; okâminakasîskâhk isiwêpinêwak. ||| They took hold of Rabbit; they threw him into the brambles.
"kitatamihinâwâw êsiwêpiniyêk!" itwêw wâpos. ||| “Very kind of you to throw me here!” said Rabbit.

kîtahtawê ê-misâk ôtênaw ayîsiyiniwak ê-wîkicik, pêyak okimâw otânisa miyosiyiwa. ||| Once upon a time in a big town where people dwelt, a certain chief had a beautiful daughter.

ê-âmaciwê-cikahkwêt kotak mîna, kâ-pimakotêyik cikahkwân. wâpahtam awa nistam kâ-âcimak. ||| When one of them, the second one, threw a throwing-stick up the hill, [sic] and it sped through the air, the one of whom first I spoke, saw it.

On all the drying-frames that are on the camp-site let them hang the meats, and for this drying-frame of yours let them take the fattest one, to provide meat for them to eat!” said the boy who was a prattler; “If they do this way and do not peep, things will always go as well as this. But if they peep, things will not go well. Even if Partridge-Claw here drives buffalo, things will go just as well, if only your father and your mother do not try to look. ha, êkoyikohk êskwâk âtayôhkêwin. ||| Well, that is the end of the sacred story.

Then the younger sister's husband got up: he turned out to be a handsome young man. Oh, she was glad, that woman. Then, after a bit, when the elder one's husband got up, he turned out to be a very old man with white hair. She did not like his being old. So then they stayed there. The men sat there all day. Only at nightfall they left the house and went away. When daybreak was near, they came back. Then they went to bed. In the morning, when they had eaten, the elder sister and the younger would always go tramping about, looking for berries and for wild turnips, for these were all they had to eat; but never did their husbands hunt. Then at one time, when they had been there quite a while, the elder sister did not recognize the land. It seemed to her as if she had never seen the land where they were. She was sad, and she disliked having for husband, as it turned out, an old man. Then she kept wandering about. And she was sad because there were no other people there where they dwelt; this it was made her sad. Then at one time, when as usual they were wandering about, digging wild turnips here and there, they saw a lodge of old leather.

ôta tastawayakap ê-wî-ati-sîpâsit, ôhi kâ-nayômâyit asiniya pakiciwêpinêyiwa. ||| When she made to go under between his legs, he dropped the stone which he was carrying.

êkwa nama kêkway tita-mîciyit. ||| But there was nothing for her to eat.

ê-kitohtât, kiyipa mostoswa kâ-pâpayiyit. ||| When he played on the flute, quickly the buffalo came running.

tapasiyiwa kahkiyaw mostoswa. ||| All the buffalo ran away.

êkosi wayawîw awa oskinîkiskwêw, ê-otinahk acosisa. ||| So the young woman went out and took up the arrows.
êkwa, "hâ, nisîm, kahkiyaw otêyaniya piko otina," itêw osîma, tâpwê awa iskwêw ê-kî-otinahk môhkomân, ê-nitawi-manisahk otêyaniya piko, kahkiyaw ê-otinahk, êkwa ê-pîhtokêt, êkwa otêyaniya ê-kîsisahk, ê-paminawasot. ||| Then, “Now, little sister, take all their tongues, but nothing more,” he told his sister, and so the woman, taking a knife, went and cut only the tongues; she took them all and came in, and cooked the tongues, preparing a meal.
êkwa awa oskinîkiskwêw ê-wayawît, ê-wî-pônahk, ôhi mihcêt kâ-nipahâyit ostêsa namwâc kêkway pimisiniyiwa. ||| But when the young woman went out to get fuel, none at all lay there of the many beasts her brother had killed.
mâmaskâtam, mihcêt ê-kî-nipahâcik mostoswa. ||| She was amazed, for they had killed many buffalo.

"haw, nisîm, osîhtâ kitayiwinisa," itêw; "niya pisisik nitatoskân miskwamîhk, tahki ê-êskêyân." "êkâya wîhkâc,- kîtahtawê awiyak ôta ta-takosin, nisîm,- êkâya wîhkâc tawinamaw awiyak, piyêyakoyini," itêw. ||| “There, little sister, make clothes for yourself,” he told her; “I am always working at the ice, making holes. Do you never for at some time someone will come here, little sister do you never open the door for anyone, when you are alone,” he told her.
tâpwê ka kâ-kaskikwâtisôw awa oskinîkiskwêw, êkwa ê-miyohot, ê-nânapâcihot. ||| So then that young woman kept sewing for herself, and then dressed in good clothes and decked herself out.
têkohtêci awa pêyakokât, miywêyihtam ê-kwayâci-paminawasoyit osîma. ||| Whenever One-Leg came home, he was glad, becuase his sister had already done the cooking.

nama wîhkâc wayawîtimihk kêkway nâtamiyiwa, âta ê-pêyakokâtêt. ||| She never had to fetch anything out of doors, even though he was one-legged.
iyikohk kêtâtwâwi otêyaniya, "hâw, nisîm, nânapâciho; wawêsî," ê-itât, kîsi-wawêsiyici, ê-miyâhkasahk okicohcikanis, "hâw, ispimihk akosî ôta wâskahikanisihk," itêw; "kitohtâ," itêw; "pâpayitwâwi mostoswak, iyikohk kahkiyaw sipwêpayitwâwi, tapasîtwâwi, ka-nîhtakosîn," itêw osîma. ||| Whenever they had eaten up the tongues, “Now, little sister, deck yourself out; put on your finery,” he would tell her; and, when she had put on her finery, and he had burned incense under his flute, “Now climb up on the roof of the house,” he would tell her; “Sound the flute,” he would tell her; “When the buffalo come, then only after all of them have gone away, after they have fled, only then you are to climb down,” he told his little sister.
êkosi miyâhkasam okicohcikanis. ||| Then he held his flute in the incense smoke.

êkwa wiya pêyakokât ê-kîsi-yôhtênahk, kitohtâyiwa, kâ-pâpahtâyit mostoswa, ê-wâskâpayiyit wîkiwâw ôma. ||| Then, when One-Leg had opened the door, she blew the flute, and the buffalo came running, circling round their dwelling.

ê-kî-akotât kicohcikanis, "nhâw, nisîmis, nîpisisa nitawi-otina," itêw. ||| After hanging up the little flute, “Now, sister, go take up my arrows,” he told her.
wayawîw, ê-nitawi-otinahk acosisa. ||| She went out and took up the arrows.

Whenever I kill game, you shall have only the tongues for your food, so highly do I esteem you, little sister,” he said to her; “When you were in piteous straits, ‘Let me befriend my little sister!’ was my thought,” he told her.
êkosi nitawi-otinam pisisik otêyaniya. ||| Acordingly, she went and took only the tongues.
"nisîm, êkâya wîhkâc wayawî." "iyâta-awiyak-wâpamaci, têkohtêci, namôya ka-wayawîn." "mihcêtiwak ayîsiyiniwak êkâ katawa ê-itâtisicik," itêw. ||| “Little sister, never go out of doors. Even though you see somebody, even though somebody comes here, you are not to go out of doors. There are many persons of evil ways of life,” he told her.
tâpwê kâ-kapê-kîsik pêyakôw awa iskwêw, wiya awa pêyakokât pisisik ê-nitawi-êskêt miskwamîhk. ||| So daily all day long the woman stayed alone, while One-Leg always went to chop holes out on the ice.
êkwa wâh-tipiskâki, ê-kîwêt awa pêyakokât, miywêyihtam kâkikê ê-kwayâci-paminawasoyit osîma. ||| And, just before nightfall, when One-Leg came home, he rejoiced that his sister always had the meal cooked and in readiness at his coming.

tâpwê kêtohtâyici, mostoswa pâpayiyiwa, ê-wâskâpayit wîkiwâhk, ê-nôcihât pêyakokât. ||| Truly, whenever she sounded it, the buffalo came, and circled round thier house, while One-Leg attacked them.

piyis mêstinam acosisa. ||| At last he had used up the arrows.

mâka pêyak awa mostos ê-wâpiskisit, mâna êwako mâna ê-pê-nîkânohtêt, êkosi êwakoni nama wîhkâc wî-nipahêw pêyakokât; êwako awa kâ-wâpiskisit mostos iskwêwa ôhi wêpahwêw, opakwahtêhoniyiw ê-tâpisi-kwâskwahamawât otêskana ohci. ||| Now, one of those buffalo, which was white, the one which always walked at the head as they came, this one One-Leg never tried to kill; and now this same white buffalo tossed the woman on its horns, pulling her up by her belt which it had caught on its horns.
kahkiyaw mostoswak tapasîwak. ||| All the buffalo fled.
kwâsihimâwa osîma, aspin ê-ati-mâtoyit. ||| His little sister was carried off, weeping afar as she disappeared from sight.

êkwa pêyakokât êkota ayâw. ||| One-Leg stayed there.
mistahi mihtâtêw osîma. ||| He mourned greatly for his little sister.
iyikohk ê-pôni-pîkiskâtât osîma, êkoyikohk osîhtâw wâskahikan, ê-ispâyik, ê-misâyik. ||| When he had passed the extreme of desolation at her absence, he built a high and great wooden house.

êkoyikohk êkwa, "mahti nisîm nika-pimitisahwâw," êkwa itêyihtam, êkwa ê-sipwêhtêt, ê-mitihtât mostoswa. ||| Then, “Let me go in pursuit of my little sister,” he thought, and set out, following the trail of the buffalo.
âta kayâs ê-kî-pimohtêyit, mâka miyo-mitihtêw. ||| Although it was a long time since they had passed, yet he trailed them with ease.
kîtahtawê, wâhyaw êkwa ê-ayât, kîtahtawê kâ-wâpahtahk sâkahikan ê-misikamâyik. ||| Presently, when he had gone a long ways, he saw a large lake.
pôti ôma kî-ministikôwiyiw, êkota kâ-mihcêtiyit mostoswa. ||| And there was an island, and on it were many buffalo.
ê-kitâpamât, kâ-wâpamât ôhi ê-wâpiskisiyit mostoswa. ||| When he looked at them, he saw the white buffalo.
piyisk otihtam sâkahikan, sisonê sâkahikanihk ê-pimisihk. ||| At last he came to the lake, and lay down by the shore of the lake.
"hâw, ôma kâ-wî-pôtâtamân ta-ati-miskwamîwiw!" itwêw. ||| “Now, let that upon which I blow continue to turn into ice!” he said.
ôma nipiy pôtâtam: âpihtaw isko miskwamîwiyiw. ||| He blew upon the water: half of the way across it turned into ice.
kîhtwâm pôtâtam: êkwa âsowakâmê-miskwamîwiyiw. ||| He blew on it again: all the way to the other shore it was ice.
kîpipayihôw, "nika-wî-âpakosîsiwin!" ê-itwêt. ||| He flung himself on the ground, saying, “Let me turn into a mouse!”
êkosi sipwêpayiw, miskwamîhk ê-pimipayit. ||| Then he ran off, running over the ice.
êkwa ita mâna ê-nâh-nitawi-minihkwêyit pisiskiwa, êkotê kâsôw, sakâhk ê-pa-pimisihk, "mâskôc pê-kwâpikêci nisîm," ê-itêyihtahk, êkwa ê-wî-kakwê-wâpamât osîma. ||| Then there where always the beasts went to drink, there he hid, lying among the trees, thinking, “Perhaps my little sister will come here to fetch water,” for he meant to try and see his little sister.
kîtahtawê kâ-wâpamât ôhi kâ-wâpiskisiyit mostoswa, ita ê-itiskwêpiyit, êkota ê-apiyit osîma, mitoni ê-kanawêyimimiht osîma. ||| Presently she saw the white buffalo and by its head, as it sat there, sat his little sister, his little sister, closely guarded.

"hâw, ôki cî mâna mostoswak kisiwâk kôy-otihtâwak?" ||| “Do you go close up to these buffalo?”
"hâw, wîcihin." "êkâya wîhtamaw awiyak ôta ê-ayâyân." "kaskihtâyani, nisîm ta-wîhtamawat ita ta-pê-itohtêt," itêw. ||| “Then help me. Tell no one that I am here. If you can manage it, tell my little sister to come here,” he told it.
"hê hê hê ha ha!" itwêyiwa; "âyiman!" "mistahi kanawêyimâw kisîm." "êkosi kwatakêyimôw kisîm," itik; "êyiwêhk mahti!" "mâka ani pakwâtam cîki awiya ta-itohtêyit," itik. ||| “Dear me, dear me!” it said; “That is difficult! Your little sister is closely guarded. Unhappy is your sister,” it told him; “But at any rate, I will try. But he does not like anyone to come near,” it told him.
êkosi sipwêhtêyiwa, konita tatâstawâyihk mostosonâhk ê-papâmipayit awa sihkos, ê-wî-kakwê-otihtât ôhi iskwêwa. ||| So it set out, that weasel, running about here, there and everywhere, between and under, through the buffalo country, trying to reach that woman.
piyis cîki ê-ayât, âsay wâpamik ôhi wâpiski-mostosa. ||| At last, when it had got near, already it had been seen by the white buffalo.
êkosi ê-ati-itohtêyit, tapasîw. ||| So, when the other came toward it, it fled.
êkwa itohtêw ôhi pêyakokâta. ||| Then it went to One-Leg.
ômisi itêw: "âyiman." "nama nikî-otihtâw kisîm." "nîsta nikostâw wâpiski-mostos," itwêyiwa; "mayaw ê-wâpamit, âsay nipê-nâtik," itik; "âyiman ani!" itik. ||| It said to him, “It is difficult. I could not reach your little sister. I too fear the white buffalo,” it said; “As soon as it saw me, it came for me,” it said to him; “It is a difficult thing!” it said to him.
kîtahtawê êkota kâ-pê-twêhoyit cahcahkâyôwa. ||| Presently a blackbird came and alighted there.
"ôma kâ-papâ-mâna-wîsâhkawacik pisiskiwak, mitoni cî kinakayâskawâwak?" ||| “When in your way you go about delighting the beasts, have you got them much used to your presence?”
ahpô mâna wâwikaniwâhk twêhôwak, âskaw ostikwâniwâhk mîna," itêw. ||| I even perch on their backs, and sometimes on their heads,” it told him.
"mâka awa wâpiski-mostos, âskaw cî mîna êwako kisiwâk kôsâpamâw?" ||| “But this white buffalo, do you sometimes see him too from close by?”
âskaw ostikwânihk otêskanihk nitwêhowân." "namôya mâna pakwâtam," itik. ||| Sometimes I settle on his head and on his horns. He does not mind,” it told him.
"hâw, kitimâkêyimin!" "wîcihin!" "nisîm ana kîmôc kakwê-wîhtamaw ôta ê-ayâyân." "nânitaw isi ta-kakwê-kwâpikêw," itêw. ||| “Then, take pity on me! Help me! Try secretly to tell my little sister there that I am here. Let her try to come somewhere to get water,” he told it.
êkosi, "êha; nika-wîhtamawâw," itêw. ||| Then, “Yes, I will tell her,” it said to him.
hâ, êkosi aspin ê-ohpihâyit, konita mêkwâ mostosonâhk papâ-ta-twêhôw awa cahcahkayow. ||| Then up it flew and away, and here and there in the buffalo land the blackbird would alight.

êkota cîki nitawi-twêhôw, konita ê-papâ-ca-cahkatahikêsit. ||| It went and alighted near by, pecking about here and there with its little beak.

kîtahtawê kâ-ohpipayihoyit, ostikwânihk ê-twêhoyit awa oskinîkiskwêw. ||| Presently it flew up and perched on the young woman's head.
namôya pisiskêyimêw, ê-wawiyatêyimât. ||| She paid no attention to it, merely thinking it pleasingly droll.
kîtahtawê otihtimanihk twêhoyiwa. ||| Presently it perched on her shoulder.
ômisi itik: "êkâya ka-sêkimitin, ê-kitocitân," itik, ohtawakâhk ê-itiskwêyiyit; "kistês takosin, 'nitawi-wîhtamaw,' ê-isit." "ôta kwâpikêskanâhk pimisin;" "'ta-kakwê-pê-kwâpikêw!' kititik." ||| Thus it spoke to her: “Let me not frighten you by speaking to you,” it said to her, holding its head close to her ear; “Your brother has come here, and ‘Go tell her,’ he has bidden me. He lies there by the path where water is fetched; ‘Let her try to come for water!’ he says to you.”
ê-tâpwêyan cî?" itêw. ||| Are you speaking true?” she asked it.
êkwa ohpihât awa, êkoyikohk pêkopayiw awa mostos. ||| When it flew up, the buffalo awoke.

kotak awiyak ta-nâtam, ta-minihkwêyan," itêw. ||| Someone else will fetch your drink,” it said to her.
ohcitaw ê-nôhtê-nitawi-minihkwêyân." "osâm ninêstosin, pêyakwanohk tahki ê-apiyân," itêw; "piyis niskâta niwî-wîsakêyihtên." "nika-isi-sâwahton," itêw. ||| What I want is to go and drink. I am weary of always sitting in one place,” she said to it; “In the end I shall have pains in my legs. Let me stretch my legs by walking a bit,” she said to it.
"ahaq." "kiyipa kakwê-takohtê;" "êkâya mîna awiyak wîcêw," itêw, ê-pakwâtahk kotaka nâpêwa ta-kitotikoyit ôhi iskwêwa awa mostos. ||| “Very well. Try to come back soon; and do not go with anyone,” it told her, for that buffalo hated any other man to talk to the woman.
"êha," itwêw awa iskwêw, ê-ati-pasikôt, ê-sipwêhtêt. ||| “Yes,” said she, and arose and went off.
tâpwê ê-otihtahk sâkahikan, "âstam, nisîm!" kâ-itikot ostêsa. ||| Really, as she came to the lake, “Come here, my little sister!” her big brother said to her.
ê-otihtât, "namôya cî awiyak kisiwâk ayâw?" itik. ||| When she came where he was, “Is no one near?” he asked her.
"â, nisîm, ê-pê-nâtitân ôma," itêw, ê-ocêmât awa iskwêw ostêsa. ||| “Now, little sister, it is that I have come to fetch you,” he said to her, as she kissed her big brother.
êkosi mîna pôtâtam ôma sâkahikan: âpihtaw isko miskwamîwiyiw. ||| So then again he breathed on the lake; halfway across it was ice.
mîna ê-pôtâtahk, êkwa akâmihk isko. ||| When he blew on it again, then all the way to the far shore.
"hâw, nisîm, kawipayiho," itêw; "nika-wî-âpakosîsiwinân." ||| “Now then, little sister, lie down on the ground,” he told her; “We shall turn into mice.”
êkwa miskwamîhk pimipayiwak. ||| Then they ran along over the ice.
kêkâc ê-kîsi-pihkohocik, êkoyikohk ati-tihkisoyiwa ôhi miskwamiya. ||| When they had got almost across, the ice began to melt.
piyisk âta wiya pihkohôwak, êkwa ê-tapasîcik. ||| At last, however, they got to the shore and made off in flight.
êkoyikohk êkwa wâpamikwak, "hayâhây! ||| But now they were seen by the others, and “Ho, ho, ho!
pêyakokât osîma kwâsihêw!" "nawaswâtihk!" ka-matwê-itwêyit mostoswa. ||| One-Leg is taking his sister away! Go after him!” they heard the buffalo cry.
êkosi êkwa sôhki pimipahtâwak osîma. ||| So then he and his sister ran fast.
kîtahtawê wâhyaw ê-ayâcik, êkwa wî-atimikwak, osâm nawac ê-yîkicikâwît awa iskwêw. ||| Presently, when they had gone a long ways, the others were near to overtaking them, for the woman was too slow on her feet.

wâwîs êwako kiyipa kitâyiwa. ||| This they devoured all the more quickly.

In the end someone would destroy you. I am too fond of you. After a time when mortal men come into being here on earth, then there in the place of the afternoon sun you will dwell. êkoyikohk ê-iskwâk âtayôhkêwin. ||| That is the end of the sacred story.
pêyak iskwêw nitawi-mônahikêw mistaskosîmina. ||| A certain woman went to dig wild turnips.

Lo, the wind died down. Why, Nanabushu was in among the bullrushes, that was what he really had seen, like people they had seemed to him. Truly sur prised was Nanabushu, for he thought that they were people when the wind was blowing hard, so it had seemed to him ; as a matter of fact, he had been dancing with the bullrushes. And so there lay Nanabushu for a long while, he was neither able to crawl nor even to get up on his feet. Accordingly he went to sleep. After he had slept for two days, he then was able to crawl, he then crawled out to the edge of the (swamp).

Kaijiki'kandank ta'kacit i'i'widi osaga'a'mowining.3 ||| THE material contained in the present volume represents part of the results obtained by the late William Jones in his work undertaken under the auspices of the Carnegie Institution during the years 1903, 1904, and 1905. During this period Dr. Jones was research assistant at the Carnegie Institution, and he was charged with the study of the Ojibwa tribes. Most of his investigations were carried on north of Lake Superior. During the year 1906, when he was still engaged in working up the results obtained during the journeys undertaken for the Carnegie Institution, he accepted a position in the Anthropological Department of the Field Museum of Natural History, Chicago.
Mldac ajipasigundcisat. "Nimama, nackaginm, ka'ijra/yayan ! mlganabatc ka/i jiyan ajra/yayan." ||| He was immediately sent to the Philippine Islands to collect and study on behalf of the Museum. He took his manuscript material along, hoping to work on it in spare moments. During his researches in the Philippine Islands he was killed by the natives, and the manuscript material lay for a long time buried in Manila. Finally the Field Museum of Natural History sent a member of its staff, Mr. S. C. Simms, to rescue Dr. Jones's collections. He also found the manuscript which, at the request of Professor Boas, was turned over to him by the Carnegie Institution for the purpose of reporting on its condition. An agreement was reached between Professor Boas and the Carnegie Institution by which the Institution undertook to contribute to the expense of printing the collections. Anlc mlsa'pana mawit au mindimoya pisindawat Wu ga'kandinit. Uglkikanima a11 mindimoya 'iY11 watacinit 4^/uu- o-cicanya8. ||| "The work presented in the following pages is the trans lation of a body of material that was taken down in text from several dialects of an Algonkin people called the Ojibwa. It was originally the purpose to bring out this translation at the same time with the text, but circum stances of various sorts have interfered with this plan : in consequence the offer of the texts for publication will be postponed. It is the plan to present with these texts a linguistic introduction dealing with the phonetics, morphol ogy, and syntax of the Ojibwa language, together with a dictionary of stems to the same. Much work has already been done toward the fulfilment of this end, but it is not yet in a form to justify its publication.
Na, mldac 'i£i/u a'kidowat nagawabinitlwat (ayani) anawisaga'a-mowat. Igiwidac anind anugrr'kitowag : "Kagu pina! kiga'i'niga'a-nan kuca kimamanan. Wawani pinagu saga'a nda," anirr'kidowag. ||| "With this translation is an introduction treating of the material culture of the Ojibwas : it will serve as a means of rendering the narratives more intelligible. The narra tives contain myth, primitive lore, sayings, and a good deal else bearing largely on the religious sentiment ; they also contain traditional matter, some of which may be classed as historical. On account of the heterogeneous character of the work, it is hardly possible to present it in an orderly sequence. The plan of the present arrange ment has been to group together as near as possible the parts that have an intimate connection ; as, for example, tales that are variants of one another, or that have elements of a similar character, or that belong psychologically in a class by themselves. For this reason it has seemed best to break up some of the long narratives as given by the informants, and to mass together such parts of them as
Kawmdac ijiminwadanziwag igi/u wasazi'kizitcig. Midac ||| deal with the same episodes. This arrangement readily offers means for an immediate comparison of the various forms in which a common tale is told.
'ici/u a/kidowat cigwa anotcigu wrrjisaga'armowad. Pajik ||| "The work is to be taken largely as an attempt to get at the religious ideas of a people from their own point of view. As this point of view can be expressed only in terms of their own language, naturally the linguistic method had to be employed in the investigation. A speaker's own words were put down in text ; and, since the object was not to find how well a narrative could be told, never was a version repeated a second time by the one who gave it. The form of the story in the text is that which the speaker told but once, at the first dictation.
ugiwabandan wasa'kunanig. "Anlc mrrma kwaya'k nln ||| Simplicity is a characteristic mark of the narratives throughout : they run along with such an even, quiet pace, that they leave an impression of dull monotony. They are told off in a matter-of-fact way, and conscious effort at rhetorical effect is feeble. The rare use of figures of speech, and the sudden turning of phrases for springing surprise, are suggestive facts, especially from the point of view of the form and construction of a narrative. Repe tition is frequent, not only of an idea, but of an expres sion : stereotyped phrases constantly recur, verbs of saying, quotatives, and introductive adverbs being especially common. Quotatives have been in some cases difficult to handle, and equally as much trouble was given by introductive adverbs.

Midac a'pi klkagwatanimitiwad awanan a11 ||| "The language of most of the material is conversational; the periods are short; sentences colloquial, seldom sustained, and often loose and incoherent. Vagueness of reference is common. The unconscious assumption on the part of the narrator that one is familiar with the background of a narrative, is one cause why so many of the statements, when taken as they stand, are unintelligible. This vague-

In a less degree, the uncertainty of the sense of a passage has been due to the delay in translation.
Mlsa iu caylgwa ugri*nan ini/u o^umisan : " Kawmina ningutci anicinabag kiki'kanimaslg tci'a*yawat?" ||| "The language is spoken in word-sentences, and the rendering in English is generally longer. In a passage capable of more than one rendering, preference is given to the shorter. The inchoative character of a verb is always present, despite the fact that it may not be expli citly expressed in the stem. This inchoative sense is not always brought out in the translation •, in particular, if the omission is not likely to interfere with the general meaning of a passage. As already stated, the English equivalent is generally longer than the original, and it has been the object to keep the length of the translation back as near as possible to that of the original. Frequently, however, the inchoative would be superfluous in the English idiom, hence in such instances it is left unexpressed in the trans lation. A common peculiarity is met with in the inception of an inchoative, a beginning-to-do or a beginning-to-be. It is enough in English to say that 'he commenced his work,' or that 'he started to grow in stature:' but it is common
"Aye8," ugri'gon Ini o'kumisan. "O'O'widi7 agamiki'tcigami ayawag Igi/u anicinabag. " "Kunaga'ka udayaslnawatug lisi/u ickuda?" ||| in Ojibwa to say that 'he began to commence his work,' or that 'he began to start to grow in stature.' The inception of this inchoative is seldom expressed in the translation.
"Aye8," ugri'gon Ini11 o'kumisan ; "Kaga't utaiyanawa Ii8i/u ickuda." ||| "It was the plan to have the translation run as near as possible with the order of the ideas of the text ; but this could not be maintained except within approximate limits. But with few exceptions, it was possible to keep the grammar of the translation close to that of the text. Where there was departure from the grammatical structure of the original, it was in cases where the sense would have been left in doubt if fidelity to syntax was adhered to : as, for example, the matter of plurality, which the Ojibwa often expressed by the use of singular nouns and verbs, but which in the translation are rendered according to sense ; or when a passive could best be rendered by an active form, a personal by an impersonal, a transitive by an intransitive. Furthermore, the inchoative character of verbs is not always shown in the translation.
O'O'widac ugri'nan Ini/u o'kumisan : "Ambasano, ninga- ||| "The language contains grammatical gender, animate and inanimate. It may be said, that, as a rule, the animate refers to everything having the quality of life and move ment ; while the inanimate refers to all things without those qualities. 'Being' or 'creature' would be a general rendering of the animate, while 'thing' would express the inanimate. It has been found best in the translation to express gender somewhat as follows : animate as masculine, unless from the context the gender is feminine; and in animate as neuter.

"Kaga kimamaji'i'k a11 alkiwanzl." ||| UI am indebted to many who have lent aid in furthering the work, - - to many Ojibwas, among whom may first be mentioned the names of five whose narratives are here in translation. By accident they all happen to be of the Bull-Head totem. First is Mrs. Marie Syrette of Fort William, Ontario. She grew up at Lake Nipigon, where dwell Ojibwas of Lake Superior, arid to which place come those that live on the height of land and along the rivers flowing towards Hudson Bay. She is well versed in the
Mlnangwana au Nanabucu kablbagimigogubanan magwa klpa'piciwa'i'tiwat Tcagaka'a'minit-uga'kwan. Midac Nana bucu kayabi a'pidci undami'tad apitclba'a'ti mi'tigo8 ; nangwana anindowiwat pamakisiwagubanan. Uwlnga moskinamagat iu minis. ||| lore of all these people. In Ojibwa she is called Kiigigepinasi'kwa ('Forever-Bird-Woman'). Next is John Pinesi (Penessi, Penassie), chief of the Fort William Ojibwas. No name is better spoken of or more widely known by the Canadian Ojibwas than that of this fine, old man. His surname comes from an abbreviation of his Ojibwa name, which is Kagige pinasi ('Forever-Bird'), and by that name he is more familiarly known. He knows the Ojibwas from Manitoulin Island to the Sault, and all that live along the north shore of Lake Superior to Grand Marais. He has been among those who live on RainyRiver, Lake of the Woods, and those who live on the height of land ; but he is more familiar with the Ojibwas that inhabit the shore country between Kanustiquia River and the Sault, for it was in this vast region that lay the scenes and experiences of his life, from childhood to old age. The third is Wasagunackang ("He-that-leaves-theImprint-of-his-Foot-shining-in-the-Snow"). He is now an old man, bent with age, living at Pelican Lake, near the Bois Fort Reservation, in Minnesota. He grew up on Rainy River, Rainy Lake, and the Lake of the Woods. The fourth is his nephew, Midasuganj ('Ten-Claw'), living at Bois Fort. He visits with the Red Lake Ojibwas on the west, and with those of Rainy River on the north and east. He is a man of middle age, of strong physique, energetic, well built, intelligent, and of the number fre quently called upon to take leading part in ceremony. The last is Madcfgabo ('Begins-to-Rise-to-his-Feet'). He is chief of the Bear Island Ojibwas of Leech Lake in Minnesota. Unfortunately but two of his narratives appear in the collection. His help was utilized in another way, in going rapidly over the whole collection to see what was familiar to his group of Ojibwas, and what was not. kackra/wat. Misa iu cigwa' ki'tagwicimawat. "Kaga't, kiga-a-camanan wa8a/u nigig kacawaniminang." ||| UgIcotJi'U'nac, "mittens 5" the usual word for mittens is mintcikawanag. The word used here is for protectors against cold, and it may refer to mittens or earprotectors', it also refers to the string of rabbit-fur that is put through the hole of the ear in order, so it is said, to keep the ear warm. The sense of this word would often seem to imply that it meant ear-warmers or ear-protectors ; but it is given as mittens, because the Ojibwa themselves regard that as the sense of the word.
